result.summary: This section gathers fragments of the lost epic Returns (Nostoi): Proclus' plot summary of the Greek heroes' voyages home from Troy, plus scattered quotations on Medea, Antiope, Telemachus and Circe, and Tantalus. The epic told of quarrels, storms, deaths and homecomings, including the murder of Agamemnon.

scenes.title: Proclus' summary of the Returns
scenes.summary: Proclus outlines the five books: the quarrel of the Atreidae, the scattered voyages home, the storm at Capherides, the journey of Neoptolemus, the murder of Agamemnon, and Menelaus' return.
scenes.stakes: The Greek leaders risk death by storm, divine anger and betrayal on their way home from Troy.

scenes.title: Medea rejuvenates Aeson
scenes.summary: A quoted line says Medea made Aeson young again with a brew of herbs.

scenes.title: Antiope betrays Themiscyra
scenes.summary: Heracles besieges Themiscyra but cannot take it until Antiope, in love with Theseus, betrays it.
scenes.stakes: Themiscyra falls to the besieger because of Antiope's betrayal.

scenes.title: Fragments on marriages and Hades
scenes.summary: Telemachus marries Circe and Telegonus marries Penelope; a line on gifts; the Returns knew no spirit Eurynomus in Hades.

scenes.title: Punishment of Tantalus
scenes.summary: Tantalus, granted any wish by the gods, asks for endless pleasures; Zeus grants it but hangs a stone over him.
scenes.stakes: Tantalus loses all enjoyment through his excess and is perpetually tormented.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic for the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus.

notable_quotes.reason: A proverb-like line on how gifts corrupt human minds and actions.

analysis.text: The Returns shows the cost of victory: quarrels, divine anger, storms and murder at home.
The poem is lost and survives only through summaries and quotations, so its plot is known mainly from Proclus' summary.

legacy.text: The Returns fed the tradition of Agamemnon's murder and Orestes' vengeance later dramatized in Aeschylus' Oresteia.

fun_facts.text: The Returns is attributed to Agias of Troezen, though Eustathius calls its author Colophonian.

language_notes.text: The Returns (Nostoi) belonged to the Epic Cycle, poems filling out the Trojan story around the Iliad and Odyssey. Only summaries and fragments survive.
Capherides: dangerous rocks off Euboea where, in tradition, Nauplius lured the Greek fleet with false beacons; Locrian Aias (Ajax the Lesser) perished in the storm.
Odysseus is the name used here by Proclus's summary; elsewhere in this translation's Homeric context he may appear as Ulysses.
"Colophonian" means from Colophon, an Ionian city; the poem was sometimes credited to a Colophonian rather than Agias of Troezen.
"Beguile" means to deceive or charm; the line says bribes and presents sway both thought and action.
The stone hung over Tantalus is one version of his punishment; the better-known one has food and water always receding from him.

context_notes.text: Proclus summarized the Epic Cycle in his Chrestomathia, our main source for the lost poems' contents.
Teiresias was the blind Theban prophet; Calchas was the Greek seer at Troy.
Achilles was dead by this point; his ghost warns the Greeks about the dangers of their voyage.
Medea, the sorceress wife of Jason, was said to restore Aeson, Jason's father, to youth with herbs.
Themiscyra was the city of the Amazons on the Thermodon; Antiope was an Amazon, and Theseus an Athenian hero.
Telemachus is Odysseus' son and Telegonus his son by Circe; this tale links the two families by marriage.

literary_notes.text: The quarrel of the brothers starts the scattering of the fleet and prepares the disasters that follow.
The ghost's prophecy hints at the coming storm and Agamemnon's murder.
The golden cauldrons and the "sweet young boy" give a vivid picture of magical renewal.
Offered any wish, Tantalus wastes it on indulgence, and his excess prepares his punishment.
The punishment fits the crime: pleasures sit near him, yet the hanging stone keeps him from enjoying them.
